identification: Australian Museum: streamlined body, bill and broad flat tail, short webbed feet, dense dark brown to reddish-brown fur with light brown/silver underfur; males typically 400–630 mm and 800–3000 g, females 370–550 mm and 600–1700 g, and males can be over 60 cm; males have an ankle spur linked to a venom gland (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria: flattened brown body, wide flat bill, webbed feet and flat tail, up to 55 cm bill to tail; sometimes mistaken for the Water Rat Hydromys chrysogaster when swimming; males have a venomous hind-foot spur (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: up to 60 cm, dark-brown bill, waterproof fur dark brown above and light brown or cream below, webbed feet, and venomous spurs on the male’s hind legs (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/).
origins: Family Ornithorhynchidae, order Monotremata; an egg-laying monotreme, with echidnas the only living monotremes (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Endemic to Australia; present in eastern Queensland and New South Wales, eastern, central and southwestern Victoria, and throughout Tasmania; extinct in South Australia except an introduced Kangaroo Island population (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria distribution: eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: widespread from Queensland to Tasmania and in almost all areas of Victoria except the Mallee (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/). Inverleigh, the Leigh River, the Barwon at Inverleigh, Teesdale, Bannockburn and Inverleigh reserves: not stated on sources opened.
habitat: Freshwater rivers, streams and other freshwater bodies, from tropical rainforest lowlands to cold high country, feeding in slow and fast water but preferring coarser cobble and gravel bottoms; burrows in earth banks, with native vegetation, logs, twigs and roots (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria: freshwater rivers and streams (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: freshwater creeks, streams, rivers and lakes, including the Yarra River in Melbourne, preferring water with twigs, roots, gravel and logs, and burrows under trees, shrubs and roots on banks (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/).
trees: Named tree species not stated. Sources describe native bank vegetation, roots, logs and stream shading rather than a preferred food tree (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/).
diet: Mainly benthic aquatic invertebrates, especially insect larvae, plus shrimps, swimming beetles, water bugs, tadpoles, worms, freshwater pea mussels and snails, and occasionally surface cicadas and moths; captive animals are often fed yabbies (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria: larval mayflies, caddisflies and small molluscs, detected with bill sensory organs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: mostly aquatic insects, also worms, small fish, shrimp and freshwater molluscs, stored in cheek pouches and ground on hard plates (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/).
breeding: In New South Wales and Victoria mating is normally August to October; females lay 1–3 eggs, usually 2, after a 21-day gestation, incubate for possibly 10 days, and lactate 3–4 months; young do not breed in their first year and many females not until at least 4 years (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria: females lay two eggs in a nursery burrow that take two weeks to hatch (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: Victorian breeding August to October; the female holds eggs between a curled tail and belly, and young stay in the nesting burrow for three months (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/). Zoos Victoria: Healesville first bred a platypus in 1943; breeding season August to November (https://www.zoo.org.au/member-zone/zoo-news/member-blog-secretive-platypus-behaviour-caught-on-camera).
activity: Active all year, mostly at twilight and night, sheltering by day in a short bank burrow (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria: nocturnal and diurnal, most often seen swimming and diving in freshwater at dusk (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Wildlife Victoria: usually feeds at night for 10 to 12 hours and rests in the burrow by day (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/).
bestViewing: Sources give general timing only: twilight and night, and Museums Victoria says most often at dusk (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). A recommended Inverleigh site is not stated on sources opened. Do not capture or kill platypuses except for scientific research (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). If handling an injured animal, pick it up by the end half of the tail because the male spur can cause severe, long-lasting pain (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Wildlife Victoria: do not touch or pick up a sick, injured or orphaned platypus; call (03) 8400 7300; keep dogs on a leash near known platypus locations; do not use opera-house nets in Victorian public waters (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/). Feeding advice is not stated on these pages.
hangouts: Named places on the ALA rows inside 5 km are the Leigh River at Inverleigh, the Barwon River at Inverleigh, and the confluence of the Barwon and Leigh Rivers. Close examples: GAP_SiteID FOTB23 Leigh River at about 0.3 km (2021, genetic water samples); Leigh River Inverleigh at about 0.5 km (2016); a platypus-survey point on the Leigh River in 2002; GAP_SiteID 99 Barwon River at about 1.1 km (2021); Barwon River: Inverleigh (1966, 900 m uncertainty); Barwon River: S of Inverleigh (1997); the confluence (cPlatypus, 2020 and 2022, about 1.5 km); and GAP_SiteID 25 Leigh River at about 3.4 km (2021), with a 2026 Australian Platypus Conservancy observation at the same upstream area. A 2025 cPlatypus note says the animal was seen at the end of Park Street. A 2023 note says it was close to the west bank beside a walking track. A 2023 row at about -38.1043, 144.0638 is a watched dive at late afternoon or dusk. iNaturalist 224575712 (24 June 2024, research, about 0.6 km, place guess Inverleigh) and 97751600 (10 October 2021, casual, about 2.2 km, accuracy 15 m) are the two observations inside 5 km. Golden Plains SLO16 names the platypus on the Leigh River (Waywatcurtan) where it meets the Barwon at Inverleigh (https://planning-schemes.app.planning.vic.gov.au/Golden%20Plains/ordinance/42.03-s16). Corangamite CMA says the Barwon flows near Inverleigh and the Leigh joins the Barwon there, and that the river is platypus habitat (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/projects/barwon-flagship-waterway/; https://ccma.vic.gov.au/waterways/waterway-management/water-for-the-environment/upper-barwon-river/). The 2024–25 water-year review records platypus citizen science at Inverleigh; it also names Winchelsea, which is outside this circle (https://ccma.vic.gov.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Water-year-review-Upper-Barwon-River-2024-25-V2.pdf). Also nearby, outside 5 km: GAP_SiteID FOTB 10 Barwon at about 6.3 km (eight repeated 2021 genetic samples); GAP_SiteID 24 Leigh at about 6.5 km; Murgheboluc at about 8.0 km (1978). Mount Pollock (1965) has 9000 m uncertainty and is not a site. A 2025 pair labelled Surf Coast LGA sits near -38.1475, 143.9926, about 7.3 km out; the LGA text is not the place. Fyansford and the Platy Patch are outside 10 km and are not used.
threats: Dependence on freshwater systems may cause future decline; anecdotal predators include crocodiles, goannas, carpet pythons, eagles, large native fish, and likely foxes, dogs or dingoes; a platypus tick and a fungal skin infection, especially in Tasmania, are reported (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Wildlife Victoria: litter and rings in waterways, illegal opera-house nets, and foxes, dogs and cats (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/platypus/).
conservation: July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List: Platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus, extinction risk Victoria, category Vulnerable (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). Museums Victoria: FFG Threatened List Vulnerable; EPBC Act 1999 Not listed; IUCN Red List Near Threatened (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8436). Australian Museum: IUCN Near Threatened, assessed 2014; protected in all states where it occurs, but EPBC and FFG categories are not stated on that page (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). The June 2024 FFG Threatened List includes Platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus, with the extracted category column aligning to Vulnerable and extinction risk Victoria (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/707416/FFG_Threatened_List_June_2024.pdf). Zoos Victoria’s World of the Platypus page labels conservation status Near Threatened, while a Zoos Victoria page states platypuses are Vulnerable in Victoria under the FFG Act 1988 (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/world-of-the-platypus/; https://www.zoo.org.au/member-zone/zoo-news/member-blog-secretive-platypus-behaviour-caught-on-camera).

identification: Australian Museum: macropod with larger hind legs, large hind feet and a long muscular tail used for balance and as a fifth limb; light grey woolly fur, darker face and a dark tail tip; males body to 1.3 m and tail to 1 m, females body to 1 m and tail to 0.84 m (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text of the species page: grey fur paler underneath, tail often black at the tip, head held high and tail curved up when hopping; body up to 1.3 m, tail up to 1.1 m; often confused with the Western Grey Kangaroo (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419). Zoos Victoria: thick fluffy fur from light grey to grey-brown, up to seven feet tall (https://www.zoo.org.au/kyabram/habitats/free-roaming-animals).
origins: Family Macropodidae, order Diprotodontia (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Found over most of the eastern states including Tasmania, from inland plains to the coast where annual rainfall is more than 250 mm, at all altitudes up to subalpine woodlands (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text: eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419). DEECA: Victoria has three kangaroo species, Red, Eastern Grey and Western Grey (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/kangaroos). Inverleigh localities: not stated on sources opened.
habitat: Semi-arid mallee scrub through woodlands, some farmland with remnant vegetation, and forest, tending to favour denser scrubs and forests (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text: grassy woodlands and forests, also parklands and golf courses (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419).
trees: Named food trees not stated. They favour grasses and will eat a range of plants, including fungi in some cases, and sometimes leaves from trees and shrubs (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419).
diet: Herbivorous grazer preferring young green grass shoots high in protein; dry grass is hard to digest; also other plants and sometimes fungi (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text: mainly grasses and herbs, sometimes leaves from trees and shrubs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419).
breeding: Australian Museum: breeding continuous with a summer peak; newborn weighs less than one gram and is born 36 days after mating; pouch young begins to leave at about 9 months and is independent at about 18 months (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text: at birth about jelly-bean size; joeys leave the pouch permanently at around 44 weeks; females start breeding at around 18 months and can breed all year, though young are mostly born in late autumn and early winter (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419).
activity: Nocturnal; large mobs gather at dusk to feed; they rest in shade and move out to graze from late afternoon to early morning (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Museums Victoria indexed text: mostly dusk to dawn, often in mobs (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8419). Zoos Victoria: most active in the evening and at dawn, but can be seen resting in shade or tall grass by day (https://www.zoo.org.au/kyabram/habitats/free-roaming-animals).
bestViewing: Late afternoon to early morning, when mobs feed in the open (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). No local Inverleigh viewing site is stated on sources opened. Wildlife Victoria: avoid driving at dawn and dusk or slow down; watch roadside vegetation; report injured or dead animals because pouch young may survive; check a pouch only after confirming the animal is dead, and call (03) 8400 7300 (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/cause-of-injury-post/driving-and-wildlife/). DEECA: kangaroos are protected (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/kangaroos). Lights and feeding advice for wild eastern grey kangaroos are not stated on these pages.
hangouts: The Friends of Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve page says the 1050 hectare reserve between Inverleigh and Teesdale has a large population of Eastern Grey Kangaroos (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). A Golden Plains panel report says the same reserve, also called the Common and formally gazetted as the Inverleigh Flora Reserve in 1988, has a large colony of Eastern Grey Kangaroos (https://goldenplains.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/Golden%20Plains%20C87gpla%20Panel%20Report%20.pdf). ALA rows inside 5 km name Inverleigh Conservation Nature Reserve (2018, about 2.2 km), Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve (2010, about 2.3 km, and 2016 at about 3.4 km), Old Shelford Track 0.75 km northwest of Carrah Track, 5.2 km south of Teesdale (1998, about 2.9 km), roughly 4 km south of Teesdale (1989, about 4.8 km), 4 km NNW of Inverleigh (1992), and Inverleigh Flora and Fauna Reserve site IFFR40 (2000 and 2002, about 4.9 km). Many 2020–2024 iNaturalist Australia rows inside 5 km have no locality string; their place guesses on the iNaturalist API include Inverleigh. Also nearby: Teesdale (undated, 4500 m uncertainty, about 6.7 km); Mason's Road, Bannockburn (2007); Bannockburn Bushland Reserve (2012 camera, about 9.4 km); and several Bannockburn species-list points about 9.6–9.7 km out. A 2018 pair near -38.184, 144.050 has one row with 28.3 km accuracy and a locality 'Victoria, AU', so that public coordinate is not a place. Teesdale Grassy Woodlands and Don Wallace Reserve are a different reserve and are not added from a Teesdale brochure.
threats: Australian Museum discusses historical hunting and licensed commercial harvest of four abundant kangaroo species, and says none of those four is threatened or endangered; it does not list current threat processes for this species (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). Wildlife Victoria: kangaroos and wallabies are among the species most often hit on roads, and the eastern grey kangaroo is the species most often reported to them as hit by a vehicle; kangaroos can travel at speeds up to 65 km/h (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/cause-of-injury-post/driving-and-wildlife/). DEECA says kangaroos sometimes require management for population health and welfare and to protect people, property and biodiversity (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/kangaroos).
conservation: July 2026 Flora and Fauna Guarantee Threatened List: no mammal entry for Macropus giganteus (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0028/793801/FFG_Threatened_List_July_2026.pdf). The 28 August 2026 EPBC extract has no row for this scientific name (https://data.gov.au/data/dataset/ae652011-f39e-4c6c-91b8-1dc2d2dfee8f/resource/78401dce-1f40-49d3-92c4-3713d6e34974/download/20260828spcs.csv). Absence of a row is not a SPRAT sentence that says the species is 'Not listed'. Australian Museum: IUCN Least Concern; protected by law; not stated as threatened or endangered among the four abundant commercially harvested species; EPBC and FFG categories are not stated on this page (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/eastern-grey-kangaroo/). The Museums Victoria species page failed to open, so its status line is not stated from an opened page. A name search of the June 2024 FFG Threatened List did not return Macropus giganteus (https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0025/707416/FFG_Threatened_List_June_2024.pdf).
notWellDocumented: Supplied ALA 26/58 matches the species facet. The 10 km year facet sums to 57 because one Teesdale row has no year. iNaturalist all grades 16/40 and research 13/35.
Do not quote the 1989 individualCount of 40 as a mob. The 2018 Victoria, AU coordinate has about 28 km accuracy.
Museums Victoria birth timing (mostly late autumn and early winter) and the Australian Museum summer peak are left unreconciled.
Sandstone is not relevant. Western Grey Kangaroo weights from other DEECA notes are not used.

identification: Australian Museum: sharp spines, short legs and long snout; size range 40–55 cm; the only echidna species in Australia; similar species is the Long-beaked Echidna Zaglossus bruijni of New Guinea (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/short-beaked-echidna/). Museums Victoria: rounded body covered in sharp spines with fur between, spines yellow-cream with black tips, smooth tubular snout, long sharp claws, body up to 44 cm (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8416). Zoos Victoria: 30–40 cm long, weight up to 2–5 kg, spines about 5 cm (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/short-beaked-echidna).
origins: Family Tachyglossidae, order Monotremata; an egg-laying mammal (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/short-beaked-echidna/). Found throughout Australia, including Tasmania (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/short-beaked-echidna/). Museums Victoria: native to Australia; mainland Australia and Tasmania; one of the largest ranges of any Australian mammal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8416). Zoos Victoria also says Papua New Guinea and Indonesia (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/short-beaked-echidna). A Victorian locality finer than the state is not stated on sources opened.
habitat: Forests and woodlands, heath, grasslands and arid environments (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/short-beaked-echidna/). Museums Victoria: almost all terrestrial habitats, including forests, and listed habitats wetland, urban, dry forest, wet forest, woodland, mallee and grassland (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8416). Zoos Victoria: bush, savannah, arid and semi-arid areas, and rainforests (https://www.zoo.org.au/healesville/habitats/koala-forest/short-beaked-echidna).
trees: Preferred trees not stated. Museums Victoria says echidnas shelter in mulch piles and sometimes leave young in backyard leaf piles (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8416).
diet: Ants and termites taken with a long sticky tongue (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/short-beaked-echidna/). Museums Victoria: ants, termites and other small invertebrates, ground on horny mouth plates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8416). identification: Museums Victoria: in southern and eastern Australia usually silver-grey above and white-cream below; thick black prehensile tail; black markings around eyes and nose; body up to 55 cm and tail up to 40 cm; call a deep guttural cough (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449). Australian Museum size range is given as 55 cm and the page says it is the familiar urban possum (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). DEECA: about the size of a cat, large pointed ears, grey fur and a bushy black tail (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums). Wildlife Victoria: up to 4 kg, cat-sized, black brush tail, generally grey with a lighter underside (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/).
origins: Family Phalangeridae, order Diprotodontia (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, Western Australia and the Northern Territory, and introduced to New Zealand (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). Museums Victoria: mainland Australia and Tasmania; native to Australia; a Central Australian subspecies is listed as Endangered in the Northern Territory, which is not a Victorian population (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449). habitat: Urban areas, forests, woodlands and heath (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). Museums Victoria: open dry eucalypt forest, woodlands and suburban areas; sleeps in tree hollows or ceilings (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449). DEECA: trees and gardens around houses provide a modified woodland (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums).
trees: Open dry eucalypt forest is named as habitat, but preferred food-tree species are not named (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449). Diet is leaves, blossoms and fruits of native and exotic trees and shrubs (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums).
diet: In the wild, leaves, blossoms and fruits; in suburbia almost anything (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). Museums Victoria: plants, leaves, fruits and flowers, sometimes nestling birds (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449). DEECA: leaves, flowers and fruits, and the brushtail may also eat grass, fungi, birds’ eggs and baby birds (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums). Wildlife Victoria: leaves, fruit, insects, bird eggs, and sometimes rubbish (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/).
breeding: DEECA: a single young born in autumn or spring; about six months in the pouch, one to two months on the mother’s back, leaving the den at 7–16 months (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums). Wildlife Victoria: breeding March to May, one joey, up to six months in the pouch then a back-rider (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/). Australian Museum and Museums Victoria pages opened do not give gestation or litter numbers.
activity: Nocturnal; by day in a hollow log, branch, trunk or another dark place, including roofs (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/). Museums Victoria: mostly active at night (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8449).
bestViewing: At night in suburban gardens and parks; only this general timing is stated (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-brushtail-possum/; https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/). No Inverleigh site is stated on sources opened. DEECA: do not feed possums, because human food can cause serious dietary imbalance; possums are protected and must not be harmed or relocated off the property; trapped brushtails must be released on the same property within 50 m after sunset on the day of capture (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums). Wildlife Victoria: do not ignore a possum on the ground in daylight; call (03) 8400 7300 (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/). Lights are not discussed on these pages.
hangouts: The reserve page says possums emerge from tree hollows at night. It does not separate brushtail from ringtail (https://inverleigh.org.au/features/nature-conservation/). identification: Australian Museum: large rodent adapted to water, webbed hind feet, waterproof coat, long white-tipped tail; flattened head, long blunt nose, abundant whiskers, small eyes and small ears; colour near-black, grey or brown above and white to orange below; body 231–370 mm, tail 242–345 mm, weight 340–1275 g (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/). Australian Museum platypus page: a swimming platypus shows three humps and no visible ears, unlike the dog-paddle of the Water-rat (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/platypus/). Museums Victoria specimen records list the preferred common name Australian Water Rat and other names Rakali, Common Water Rat and Golden-bellied Water Rat, but those records are specimens, not a species-biology page (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/specimens/128398).
origins: Family Muridae, order Rodentia, a placental rodent (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/). Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, south-west and north Western Australia, and the Northern Territory (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/). The Australian Museum does not say it is endemic only to Australia. Inverleigh localities: not stated on sources opened.
habitat: Permanent fresh or brackish water; one of Australia’s two amphibious mammals, with the platypus; burrows on river and lake banks, usually hidden in vegetation, with a round entrance about 15 cm across (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/).
trees: Not stated on the Australian Museum page.
diet: Large insects, crustaceans, mussels, fishes, frogs, lizards, small mammals and water birds; prey is caught underwater and taken to a regular feeding site (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/).
breeding: Not stated on the Australian Museum page opened.
activity: Most active around sunset and may forage during the day, unlike many native rodents that are strictly nocturnal (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/).
bestViewing: Around sunset, and sometimes by day; only this general timing is stated (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/water-rat/). No Inverleigh site is stated on sources opened. The species page does not give handling, dog, light or feeding rules. identification: Australian Museum: about cat-sized, grey with white patches behind the eyes and on the belly, orange-brown on tail and limbs, white-tipped prehensile tail; body and tail each 300–350 mm, weight 700–1100 g; sometimes confused with the Black Rat, which has different teeth, ears and tail (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-ringtail-possum/). Wildlife Victoria: less than 1 kg, about a young kitten (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/possums/).

Predominantly Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania and South Australia (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/common-ringtail-possum/). Museums Victoria: forest, coastal scrub and suburban places; the drey is a ball of small branches, grasses and leaves in the crown of trees (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8447). DEECA: dreys several metres above the ground; ringtails rarely enter house roofs (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/managing-wildlife/possums).

identification: Australian Museum: short, stocky and barrel-shaped, broad head, small eyes, powerful shoulders, tail about 25 mm hidden by fur; large naked nose, coarse coat and short rounded ears; coat colour varies widely; only two upper incisors, which keep growing; distinguished from hairy-nosed wombats by the hairless nose, coarser hair and narrower nasal bones; mainland average head-body 985 mm (840–1150 mm) and weight 26 kg (22–39 kg) (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria: grey-brown to black, broad head, large nose and ears, body up to 1.1 m (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460). Wildlife Victoria: short legs, small ears, stocky; adult length about one metre and weight 20–40 kg; backward-facing pouch (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/).
origins: Family Vombatidae, order Diprotodontia; a marsupial, not related to badgers, beavers, pigs or bears (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Historically most of Victoria except the north-western corner; today almost disappeared from the western half of Victoria, and absent from many former parts of New South Wales; also south-eastern Queensland historically, south-eastern South Australia, Tasmania, and now only Flinders Island among Bass Strait islands (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria: south-eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460). Wildlife Victoria: mainly the south-eastern areas of Victoria (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/). Inverleigh localities: not stated on sources opened.
habitat: Temperate forest of south-eastern Australia, often mountainous; avoids rainforest; in South Australia and Tasmania also woodland, coastal scrub and heath; burrows on slopes above creeks and gullies, feeding in grassy clearings (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria: dry and wet forest, woodland and coastal heath (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460). Wildlife Victoria: dug burrows that can be up to 30 metres long (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/).
trees: Not a tree specialist. Australian Museum names Tussock Grass in forest and Kangaroo Grass and Wallaby Grass in more open country, plus dry leaves, stalks, occasional bark, and in some habitats mosses (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Wildlife Victoria: herbivorous plants, roots and bark from native trees, without naming the trees (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/).
diet: Fibrous native grasses, sedges and rushes; preferred grasses as above; occasional bark and reported fungi (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria diet category: grasses (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460).
breeding: Australian Museum: one young at any time of year; gestation probably 30 days; pouch life 6–10 months, then 8–10 months with the mother; sexual maturity after two years; wild lifespan up to 11 years (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria: in winter, females give birth to a single young (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460). Wildlife Victoria: any time, most commonly November to July; gestation one month; pouch about 10 months then 8–10 months with the mother; one joey every two to three years (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/).
activity: Australian Museum: mainly nocturnal in summer, emerging when air cools, but known to forage by day in cool or overcast weather; about two thirds of life is spent in the burrow (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). Museums Victoria: largely nocturnal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8460). Wildlife Victoria: mainly crepuscular and nocturnal; daytime activity is unusual except in cooler months (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/).
bestViewing: After sunset, with longer daytime foraging on cool or overcast days (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/bare-nosed-wombat/). No Inverleigh site is stated on sources opened. Wildlife Victoria: slow down in wombat territory; report even dead wombats because a joey may be in the pouch; for mange, photograph the animal and call 03 8400 7300 rather than catching it; treatment described is pole-and-scoop or a burrow flap, without touching the animal (https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/native-species-post/wombat/; https://wildlifevictoria.org.au/learn/cause-of-injury-post/mange/). identification: This object is the name Petaurus breviceps as it appears on one local record, not a second studied species. The Australian Museum says the animal long called the Sugar Glider was split into three species: Petaurus breviceps now only on the coastal side of the Great Dividing Range, Petaurus ariel across northern Australia, and Krefft's Glider Petaurus notatus in eastern and northern Australia. All three glide on a membrane, up to 50 m (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/sugar-glider/). Museums Victoria says Krefft's Glider is the only one of the three in Victoria (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8445).
origins: Family Petauridae. The Australian Faunal Directory still has a Petaurus breviceps page that has been flagged against the P. notatus page, which says P. breviceps replaces P. notatus in coastal New South Wales and south-eastern Queensland, and which includes Victoria for P. notatus (https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Petaurus_notatus). Inverleigh is on the Victorian Volcanic Plain, west of the Divide. The credible local glider in the Atlas is Krefft's Glider.
habitat: Not stated for this name at Inverleigh. Forest and woodland hollows are described on the Sugar Glider and Krefft's Glider pages for the glider group, not for this one row (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/sugar-glider/; https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8445).
trees: No tree species is named on the Murgheboluc record. The current Australian Museum Sugar Glider page names tree hollows and not a tree species (https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/sugar-glider/).
diet: Not taken from the coastal Sugar Glider account. Museums Victoria's diet for the Victorian Krefft's Glider is gums, nectar, pollen and invertebrates (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8445). That diet is not attached to this P. breviceps row.
breeding: Not documented for this record. July to August births on the Museums Victoria page are for Petaurus notatus.
activity: Gliders on these pages are nocturnal (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8445). That is the group pattern, not a timed local sighting. The iNaturalist observation is casual and gives no time of day in the fields stored here.
bestViewing: Do not treat a casual photograph labelled Sugar Glider as an identification. Museums Victoria notes that the eyes can reflect pale red, which is an identification remark, not an invitation to spotlight (https://collections.museumsvictoria.com.au/species/8445). The local trace is one 2020 club record at Murgheboluc and one 2026 casual iNaturalist observation at Teesdale.
hangouts: One ALA row, outside 5 km: December 2020, Geelong Field Naturalists Club, human observation, count 1, locality Murgheboluc, about 7.6 km, no uncertainty stored. identification: A large fruit bat, not a microbat, and distinguishable from the insectivorous species above by size, a fox-like face, and the absence of echolocation. Australian Museum: alternative name Fruit Bat; family Pteropodidae; size 23–28 cm; one of the largest Australian bats; wingspan over 1 m; mostly grizzled, with a grey head and an orange-red mantle encircling the neck; does not echolocate; uses sight and smell. Wildlife Victoria: the most common Victorian flying-fox is Pteropus poliocephalus; up to 1.1 kg; wingspan up to one metre; black wings, grey-black body fur, an orange ruff, and a lighter grey head. Zoos Victoria Kyabram main-trail text: “The Grey-headed Flying Fox is a megabat, and the largest species of bat in Australia, weighing up to one kilogram.” The scientific name is not in that Kyabram sentence. Australian Museum also prints “NSW Conservation Status: Vulnerable”, which is a New South Wales status.
origins: Family Pteropodidae (Australian Museum; AFD breadcrumb PTEROPODIDAE). AFD: Distribution States “Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania, Victoria.” Extra distribution information: “Central QLD to Adelaide, SA, mostly within ~300 km of coastline but recent colony established in Curlwaa, NSW; Occasional individuals found on islands in Bass Strait.” IBRA includes Victorian Midlands (VM) and Victorian Volcanic Plain (VVP). Ecological descriptors: “Closed forest, coastal, gregarious, mellivore, subtropical, volant.” Extra ecological information: “Arboreal roosts, partial winter migration.” Australian Museum: colonies along the east coast from Adelaide, South Australia, through Victoria, New South Wales and Queensland, and some in the Australian Capital Territory. Wildlife Victoria: eastern Australia from north Queensland along the east coast to south-east South Australia; in Victoria, recorded across most regions, with fewer in the northwest.
habitat: Australian Museum: forests and woodlands, rainforests, intertidal mangroves and swamps, and increasingly urban colonies. Wildlife Victoria questions page: roosts are often tall trees close to water, including streamside trees, rainforests, mangroves, town parks and botanic gardens. Camps may be permanent, seasonal or occasional. Victorian camps are described as more permanently occupied, especially urban ones. Wildlife Victoria names roosting at Yarra Bend, on Wurundjeri Country. AFD: arboreal roosts; closed forest; coastal.
trees: Camp trees are described generally rather than as a single species. Wildlife Victoria: more than 100 species of native trees, plus introduced trees; favourite blossoms are eucalypts, and also paperbarks, grevilleas and banksias; garden figs and lilly pilly are eaten. Australian Museum: fruit, especially figs; nectar and pollen, especially gum trees. A Museums Victoria phrase “coastal stringybark” was on a collections page that was not fully reopened, so it is not used as a measured habitat claim. Curlwaa, NSW, is an AFD locality for a colony, not a local viewing site.
diet: Nectar, pollen and fruit. Wildlife Victoria: forage on nectar, pollen and fruit; eucalypt blossom is the favourite, also paperbarks, grevilleas and banksias; garden figs and lilly pilly; they spit pulp. Australian Museum: fruit, especially figs; nectar and pollen, especially gum trees. AFD ecological descriptor: mellivore. Australian Museum: pollinators and seed dispersers. Wildlife Victoria: most foraging is within about 20 km of camp, and animals can travel up to 100 km; Australian Museum says they may travel up to 50 km from the colony.
breeding: Two opened accounts are quoted separately. Australian Museum: breeding September–January; pregnancy about six months; the young is carried for the first three weeks, then left in crèches; flies at about three months; independent at five to six months. Wildlife Victoria: mating in autumn; conception in March and April; a single pup about six months later in spring; the mother carries it for about the first month; it flies by about three months and is weaned at about six months. A heat-stress PDF that mentions October–December births was not fully opened and is not used.
activity: Nocturnal foraging from day camps. Australian Museum: leave the colony around sunset; camps of many thousands (in the past, millions). Wildlife Victoria: nomadic across eastern Australia; researchers found animals travel on average about 1,500 km a year. AFD: partial winter migration; gregarious; volant. They do not echolocate (Australian Museum).
bestViewing: Watch the dusk departure from a camp, from a distance. Wildlife Victoria names Yarra Bend. The Victorian camps page that appears in search results (camp counts for Yarra Bend and other camps) was not opened, so those counts are not repeated. Do not enter a camp, and do not handle a grounded animal. Never handle a flying-fox. Wildlife Victoria health page (https://www.wildlife.vic.gov.au/our-wildlife/flying-foxes/flying-foxes-and-your-health): they are “best admired from a distance.” Australian bats, including flying-foxes and microbats, are natural hosts of Australian bat lyssavirus; treat all bats as if they carry it. Transmission risk named there is bites, scratches, saliva or neural tissue; blood, urine and faeces are not known to transmit ABLV. The same page: flying-foxes are a natural host of Hendra virus, which is severe or fatal in horses; human infection is very rare and has mostly followed close contact with infected horses in Queensland and northern New South Wales; flying-fox-to-human, human-to-human, and human-to-horse transmission has not been documented; Hendra has not yet been detected in Victoria. The Australian Museum species page does not mention Hendra or ABLV. Better Health Channel, https://www.betterhealth.vic.gov.au/health/conditionsandtreatments/Australian-bat-lyssavirus, title “Australian bat lyssavirus infection”: ABLV is a rare, fatal central-nervous-system disease closely related to rabies. The page says any bat in Australia could potentially carry the virus, and that the virus has been found in fruit bat, flying-fox and insect-eating microbat species. Quoted sense of the page: “Any bat in Australia can potentially carry and spread the virus.” Anyone bitten, scratched, or exposed to saliva should wash the wound and seek medical care urgently, regardless of rabies vaccination, how small the wound is, or whether the animal looks unwell. Wash with soap and water for at least 15 minutes, then apply an antiseptic with anti-viral action (povidone-iodine, iodine tincture, aqueous iodine, or ethanol). Preventive treatment with rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin may be recommended. Only people who are trained and vaccinated against rabies should handle bats. Pre-exposure vaccination is three doses of rabies vaccine; the page says the Department of Health funds the initial course, up to three doses, for volunteer Australian wildlife handlers. Four human cases are described since 1996 (three in Queensland, one in New South Wales), all after bites or scratches, all fatal. identification: Public separation of Vespadelus is unreliable from a fly-past. Australian Museum species pages for the forest bats give no colour or forearm and do not say that echolocation calls are required. Museums Victoria (collections): fur brown to grey-brown, paler underneath; ears with white projections (tragus); raised forehead; brief identification “tiny brown bat with white projections on its ears”; wingspan up to 15 cm; body up to 5 cm. Melbourne Museum wild page: weight 3.5–6 g, body 3.4–4.8 cm, tail 2.7–3.5 cm; “body no larger than a thumb”; prey located with sound; ultrasound usually too high for human ears. In-hand separation is what the sources describe for this genus. Australian Museum Technical Reports (1992) No. 8 (Parnaby; then placed in Eptesicus) states that easy or accurate field identification is not possible for many south-eastern microbats because reliable external diagnostic characters are not known, that female Eptesicus were excluded from the external key, and that voucher specimens are needed to confirm identifications. On that guide, Eptesicus vulturnus (“Pale Eptesicus”) “is most likely to be confused with” Eptesicus pumilus, which “has much darker fur colour than E. vulturnus; averages larger in size; has an angled penis”. Those 1992 names pre-date current Vespadelus usage on the Australian Museum and the Australian Faunal Directory.
origins: Family Vespertilionidae (Australian Museum; Australian Faunal Directory breadcrumb VESPERTILIONIDAE). Australian Faunal Directory current name Vespadelus vulturnus (Thomas, 1914), common name Little Forest Bat, CAVS 1379. AFD Distribution States: “Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Victoria”. Tasmania is absent from that States line. The holotype is from Tasmania, and the IBRA list includes Flinders (FLI) as well as Victorian Volcanic Plain (VVP) and Victorian Midlands (VM). Ecological descriptors: “Predator, volant, woodland.” Extra ecological information: “Solitary or social, roosts include old buildings, hibernates.” Museums Victoria collections page: “south-eastern mainland Australia and Tasmania”. That Tasmania statement is broader than the AFD States line.
habitat: Australian Museum: hunts through forests. Museums Victoria wild page: eucalypt forests of south-eastern Australia, entering farmland and townships at night. Collections page: forest and woodland. AFD ecological descriptor: woodland.
trees: Roost-tree species are not named beyond eucalypts and old trees. Australian Museum: hollows in old trees; also buildings and timber stacks; colonies up to 50; some share a nest with possums. diet: Australian Museum: small insects, taken on the wing; may land on trees for large prey. Museums Victoria wild page: only flying insects, caught on the wing.
breeding: Australian Museum: one baby in summer; females carry the baby while hunting, then leave it in the roost. Museums Victoria wild page: a single young in spring or early summer; milk for 6–7 weeks.
activity: Museums Victoria: nocturnal. Melbourne Museum wild page: enters torpor when cold. Australian Faunal Directory extra ecological information: hibernates. Australian Museum describes agile hunting on the wing.
bestViewing: A dusk fly-out may show a very small bat. These pages do not give a way to separate it from other Vespadelus in flight. Ultrasound is usually too high for human ears (Museums Victoria). Do not handle. Separation from other Vespadelus is an in-hand task on the 1992 Australian Museum guide, then under Eptesicus. That guide says reliable field-identification criteria have yet to be determined for some Eptesicus, and that females of E. darlingtoni and E. regulus “can be very difficult to distinguish”. It says males differ by penis shape: “The short bent penis of E. darlingtoni contrasts with the pendulous penis of E. regulus”. “Eptesicus regulus is smaller, forearm mostly less than 34 mm. Females with forearms larger than 36 mm, and males larger than 35 mm are probably not E. regulus. While most male E. darlingtoni have forearms larger than 34 mm, but occasionally are as small as 33.5 mm, most male E. regulus are less than about 33 mm.” “Fur colour of E. darlingtoni is often dark grey compared to the lighter brown colour of E. regulus.” The PDF text extraction rendered “forearms” as “foreanns” in two places; the figures 34, 36, 35, 33.5 and 33 mm are those in the guide. These are 1992 in-hand characters, not a public field guide for a flying animal.
